newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS - Weak prices, quota indiscipline haunt OPEC.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Weak prices, quota indiscipline haunt OPEC.

text.p: OPEC ministers gathered in Vienna on Monday to air the vexed issue of the violations of their cartel quotas that now threaten to send world oil prices skidding to the bargain basement again.

An early arrival for a conference that opens on Wednesday was the minister of Iran, Gholamreza Aqazadeh, who has called for discipline among the 11 fractious members of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC).
But neither delegates nor independent analysts see much prospect of a reduction of some two million barrels per day of OPEC supply in excess of an agreed limit of 25.03 million.

Low stocks, cold weather and delays to resumed Iraqi oil sales late in 1996 had lifted prices to post-Gulf War highs around $25 per barrel. But the oil companies have replenished their stocks and prices are now below $18.

Even so, delegates doubted if OPEC would do more than nod through a further extension of current quotas, with some pious words from its compliance committee which meets on Tuesday ahead of the conference itself.
Another early arrival in Vienna was Venezuela's Erwin Arrieta who is alleged by monitors to have abandoned any restraint and to be above quota by 800,000 barrels a day.
Arrieta said "no" when lobby reporters asked if his country, one of those that founded OPEC in 1960, would press at this meeting to scrap quotas altogether.
But he added that "we want to widen the spectrum to consider other aspects...We want to find spaces where there will be room for all producers"
"The main act in the oil sector is not OPEC,"
That appeared to be a reference to a plan to restructure OPEC on regional lines in a way that would, in effect, free Venezuela to sell as much as it wanted to the United States.
OPEC linchpin Saudi Arabia is cool to that idea and Western industry officials believe it is a non-starter.
The Saudis, who have a huge quota of 8.0 million barrels, with Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates, form a core of big Gulf Arab sellers who support oil prices by adhering to limits.
Venezuelan state oil company Petroleos de Venezuela has called for OPEC to stop using quotas to try to defend prices and to opt instead for a strategy of increasing market share to boost revenues.

Among OPEC-watchers, Peter Gignoux, head of the London energy desk at Smith Barney, pointed to present delays over continuing U.N.-supervised Iraqi oil sales as a more potent factor in support of prices than the activities of OPEC.
"Iraq is this month's swing producer. It is the only one to be witholding oil from the market. I haven't seen a willingness among the others to join the Iraqi side," Gignoux said.
